name: Lumbosacral roots L2–S1
summary: The lumbosacral roots descend obliquely from the conus as the cauda equina before leaving through their foramina, so a posterolateral disc at one level compresses the root that has not yet exited (the L4–L5 disc compresses L5, the L5–S1 disc compresses S1) while a far-lateral disc catches the root above. Each root has a bedside signature: L2–L3 hip flexion and anterior thigh; L4 knee extension, foot inversion, the knee jerk and the medial leg; L5 dorsiflexion, great toe extension, hip abduction and the dorsum of the foot; S1 plantar flexion, hip extension, the ankle jerk and the lateral foot and sole. L5 and S1 radiculopathies account for most sciatica.

anatomy.location: Roots leaving the conus at T12–L1 and descending in the cauda equina to their foramina; the exiting root passes below the pedicle of the same-numbered vertebra, the traversing root of the next level crosses the disc.

subdivisions.name: L2–L3
subdivisions.note: iliopsoas, adductors, quadriceps (partly); anterior and medial thigh

subdivisions.name: L4
subdivisions.note: quadriceps, tibialis anterior (inversion component); knee reflex; medial leg to the medial malleolus

subdivisions.name: L5
subdivisions.note: extensor hallucis longus, tibialis anterior, peroneals, gluteus medius, hamstrings (partly); no reliable reflex (medial hamstring); dorsum of the foot, great toe, lateral leg

subdivisions.name: S1
subdivisions.note: gastrocnemius, soleus, gluteus maximus, hamstrings; ankle reflex; lateral foot, sole, posterior calf

function: Segmental motor, sensory and autonomic supply to the lower limb and perineum.

bestView.label: cord (the lumbosacral roots lie in the lumbar canal, below the MNI volume)

imaging.normalAppearance: Peripheral nerves of the limbs are outside the MNI brain volume; no atlas mesh is shown. Ultrasound and MR neurography image the nerve directly; electrodiagnosis localizes the lesion functionally. Lumbar MRI shows the disc herniation, lateral recess or foraminal stenosis and its relation to the exiting and traversing roots; root enhancement suggests inflammation.

pathology.finding: Posterolateral L4–L5 or L5–S1 protrusion compressing the traversing L5 or S1 root in the lateral recess.
Compression of the exiting root (L4 at L4–L5) in the foramen.
Trefoil canal with crowded roots and neurogenic claudication.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Lumbar MRI; EMG including paraspinal muscles

lesionEffects.deficit: Sciatica to the great toe, weak dorsiflexion and great toe extension, weak hip abduction (Trendelenburg), reflexes preserved
Sciatica to the lateral foot, weak plantar flexion and absent ankle jerk
Anterior thigh pain, weak knee extension and absent knee jerk
Bilateral leg pain on walking relieved by sitting
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lumbar canal stenosis compressing several roots

examination: Straight-leg raise (L5, S1) and femoral stretch (L2–L4)
Key muscles: extensor hallucis longus (L5), toe-stand (S1), knee extension (L4)
Dermatomes: medial leg L4, dorsum L5, lateral foot S1
Hip abduction for L5 (gluteus medius, spared in peroneal palsy)
pearls: Foot drop with weak hip abduction and inversion is L5; with normal abduction and inversion it is the peroneal nerve
The ankle jerk belongs to S1 and the knee jerk to L4; L5 has no convenient reflex

pitfalls: The Z-Anatomy source models one root and ganglion pair per intervertebral foramen from C2 to L2 only, so the lumbosacral root meshes hold the L1 and L2 pairs; the L3 to S5 roots are represented by the cauda equina mesh instead.

The source also draws every root as a short straight segment running out to the foramen at its own vertebral level, so it does not show the long oblique descent that makes a paracentral disc compress the traversing rather than the exiting root.
